reasons.rubric: Predicate is a clean yes/no with an existing issuer (employer), but frequency is low (annual renewal) and landlords often want salary too, so a 3 for needing design and employer-side adoption.
reasons.validity: Renewal re-checks are plausible but not clearly common in Taiwan, and employment status alone may not satisfy a landlord who wants income evidence.
reasons.coherence: Moment, predicate, issuer and revocation fit together well; the idea honestly notes the salary gap.
reasons.novelty: Close to the known rental case but adds a new issuer (employer) and a freshness predicate on the renewal moment.
reasons.provenance: The borrowed over-collection pattern is generic and the idea reads the same without it, so it is decorative.
reasons.retention_law: A private landlord has no obvious duty to retain the full payslip or ID, though I cannot confirm Taiwanese rules.
reasons.linkability: A status token from one employer shown to one landlord has little cross-context linkage risk.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Employers have little incentive to build a revocable status service for tenants' landlords, especially small firms.
reasons.no_wallet: Landlords and small agencies are unlikely to run verifiers and many employers lack wallet-capable HR systems.

reasons.rubric: Predicate is an aggregate over filtered transactions from a single bank, which is a more complex computation, with low frequency, so a 2 to 3 band; scored 2 because use is rare and courts rely on bank certificates.
reasons.validity: Payment disputes in mediation are real, but courts accept bank certificates and the payee is disclosed anyway, so a ZK proof adds little decision value.
reasons.coherence: Parts fit, and the idea candidly admits the court-acceptance limit and payee disclosure.
reasons.novelty: No known case touches dispute evidence or transaction-sum proofs, so this is a new moment.
reasons.retention_law: Mediators and courts may need to keep the evidence submitted, though a proof could still replace full statements; unsure of the rules.
reasons.linkability: A one-off proof to a mediator in a single dispute has little linkability exposure.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Banks already issue transaction certificates on request and have little reason to sign custom aggregate attestations.
reasons.no_wallet: Mediation committees and clerks have no verifier infrastructure and parties would need wallet tooling for a one-off need.

reasons.rubric: Threshold predicate is simple but the issuer is a platform session via zkTLS with no sanctioned signing, and volume is low, so a 2.
reasons.validity: Priority slots for proven online sellers is a niche and speculative moment, and zkTLS over a seller session may breach platform terms.
reasons.coherence: The borrowed sealed-bid and voting ideas do not fit a threshold proof, and the idea itself notes a lottery removes the need.
reasons.novelty: Seller verification is a known case, but the market-slot application and zkTLS issuer are new.
reasons.provenance: The sealed-bid and ballot-separation analogies are decorative, since the idea would read the same without them.
reasons.retention_law: Organizers have no evident duty to keep seller revenue data, so the data could be dropped.
reasons.linkability: A threshold proof from a session shows little linkability, though it could reveal the shop identity.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Platforms are not signing anything and may object to zkTLS proofs from seller sessions.
reasons.no_wallet: Small organizers are unlikely to run a verifier, and applicants do not have the tooling.

reasons.rubric: Non-membership is a clean boolean, but no queryable register or signed absence attestation exists and frequency is low, so a 2.
reasons.validity: Pet hotels do not routinely screen against a ban list and no register is available to them, so the moment is thin.
reasons.coherence: The idea fits together but depends on an authority publishing an attestation that does not exist, which the idea itself admits.
reasons.novelty: Pet and animal-welfare screening is untouched by known cases.
reasons.retention_law: Shelters keep ID mainly for contact, and no stated duty to retain the full document, though I cannot confirm.
reasons.linkability: A non-membership proof is unlikely to link much, though a fixed issuer attestation could be reused.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: The authority would need legislative backing and has no incentive to publish absence attestations for private operators.
reasons.no_wallet: Small pet businesses are unlikely to operate verifiers or wallets.

reasons.rubric: Predicate is a simple current-employee boolean with an existing issuer and higher frequency, but the vendor usually has accounts already and needs the employer to sign tokens, so a 3.
reasons.validity: Staff-rate partnerships are real and the vendor needs only current employment, though many already keep a member name and payment details.
reasons.coherence: Moment, predicate, revocation and unlinkability fit together and the caveat about member accounts is honest.
reasons.novelty: Employer-issued group membership for perks is untouched by the known list.
reasons.provenance: The cookie-linkability analogy is loosely relevant but the HIPAA minimum-necessary borrowing is decorative, and the idea reads the same without them.
reasons.retention_law: A gym or clinic may need to retain customer records for its own services, though not the employer badge; unsure.
reasons.linkability: The unlinkable group proof is the central benefit and works if presentations are not tied to a stable token.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Employers must run a daily status signer to benefit a partner perk, which is of little use to them.
reasons.no_wallet: Front-desk staff need a verifier and employees need a wallet, a high bar for a small discount.

reasons.rubric: Predicate is a scoped nullifier on a high-frequency moment, but the carrier issuer is unmotivated and SIM farming makes it partial, so a 3.
reasons.validity: Promo abuse is real, but a carrier-signed credential only proves one SIM, which is cheaply multiplied, so it is not sufficient for the decision.
reasons.coherence: The idea contradicts itself slightly in stating the telco learns nothing only if blinded and then citing the opposite pull of SIM rules; otherwise it fits.
reasons.novelty: Close to the known one-person-one-account Sybil case, with a new issuer and a promotion moment.
reasons.provenance: The blind-token borrowing shapes the predicate and the SIM rule borrowing supports the issuer choice, so these are partly used rather than decorative.
reasons.retention_law: Apps have no known duty to retain phone numbers or ID photos, so the data could be dropped.
reasons.linkability: Service-scoped pseudonyms reduce cross-service linkage if issuance is blinded.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Carriers gain nothing from signing credentials for other firms' free-trial control.
reasons.no_wallet: Apps can embed verification in-app, though users need a wallet-capable carrier credential.

reasons.rubric: Absence predicate is boolean, but registers are legally restricted and the screening is of doubtful permissibility, so a 2.
reasons.validity: The idea concedes private landlords are generally not entitled to ask about such registers, which undermines the moment.
reasons.coherence: The pieces fit as a less-intrusive alternative to a criminal record certificate, but combining a sex-offender register and protection orders blurs the predicate.
reasons.novelty: Close to the known rental case with a clean criminal record, with a narrower predicate.
reasons.retention_law: Landlords have no clear duty to retain the full certificate, but the disclosure restrictions are the main issue and I cannot cite them.
reasons.linkability: Absence proofs from a government issuer are low linkability, though the issuance act itself reveals a request.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Police and the judiciary are unlikely to sign attestations for private screening given disclosure limits and rehabilitation concerns.
reasons.no_wallet: Landlords and shared-housing operators have no verifier, though platforms might provide one.

reasons.rubric: Same scoped-nullifier predicate as b03-5 with the same carrier-issuer and low-demand problems, so a 3.
reasons.validity: The idea itself says platforms accept abuse as marketing cost and have other signals, so demand is weak.
reasons.coherence: Fits together, but the onion-routing borrowing does not map to a single-hop nullifier credential.
reasons.novelty: Near duplicate of b03-5 and close to the known Sybil one-account case.
reasons.provenance: The onion-routing split-knowledge analogy and the cookie analogy are decorative since the nullifier design stands without them.
reasons.retention_law: Platforms have no evident duty to keep phone numbers or national IDs for promotions.
reasons.linkability: Platform-scoped nullifiers avoid cross-platform linking if the carrier cannot see usage.
reasons.issuer_unwilling: Carriers have little incentive to issue per-person credentials for promotion control.
reasons.no_wallet: Platforms can embed a verifier, but users need a carrier credential in a wallet.
